notes:
1. Gupta Empire — Overview

  • The Gupta Empire emerged in northern India during the early fourth century CE.
  • It became one of the most influential political powers of ancient India.
  • Major centres of Gupta power included:
  • Magadha.
  • Prayaga.
  • Pataliputra.
  • At its height, Gupta authority extended across much of northern and central India and into western India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Guptas → c. 4th–6th Century CE

2. Gupta Period and the "Golden Age"

  • The Gupta period is traditionally described as a "Golden Age" of ancient India because of major achievements in:
  • Literature.
  • Science.
  • Mathematics.
  • Astronomy.
  • Art.
  • Architecture.
  • Modern historians use this label cautiously because prosperity and social advantages were not necessarily shared equally by all sections of society.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

"Golden Age" → Traditional Description, Not Proof That Every Social Group Prospered Equally

3. Gupta Dynasty — Major Rulers

Important Gupta rulers include:

  • Sri Gupta.
  • Ghatotkacha.
  • Chandragupta I.
  • Samudragupta.
  • Chandragupta II.
  • Kumaragupta I.
  • Skandagupta.

4. Sri Gupta

  • Sri Gupta is generally regarded as the earliest known founder of the Gupta ruling family.
  • He used the title Maharaja.
  • His exact territorial extent is uncertain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Earliest Known Gupta Ruler → Sri Gupta

5. Ghatotkacha

  • Ghatotkacha succeeded Sri Gupta.
  • He also used the title Maharaja.
  • The Guptas were still a relatively regional political power during his period.

6. Chandragupta I

  • Chandragupta I transformed the Guptas into a major political power.
  • His reign is generally placed around the beginning of the fourth century CE.
  • He assumed the higher title Maharajadhiraja.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandragupta I → Maharajadhiraja

7. Gupta Era

  • The Gupta Era begins in 319–320 CE.
  • It is commonly associated with the accession or political elevation of Chandragupta I.
  • The exact circumstances of its foundation remain debated.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gupta Era → 319–320 CE

8. Kumaradevi

  • Chandragupta I married Kumaradevi.
  • She belonged to the Lichchhavi family.
  • The marriage significantly increased the political prestige of the Guptas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chandragupta I + Kumaradevi → Lichchhavi Alliance

9. King–Queen Coins

  • Gold coins depict Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi together.
  • The name of the Lichchhavis is prominently mentioned.
  • These coins demonstrate the political importance of the marriage alliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandragupta I–Kumaradevi → Joint Coins

10. Samudragupta

  • Samudragupta succeeded Chandragupta I.
  • He greatly expanded Gupta political influence.
  • His reign is one of the best documented periods of early Gupta history.

11. Main Source for Samudragupta

The most important source is:

  • Prayaga Prashasti.
  • Also called Allahabad Pillar Inscription.
📌 Must-Memorise

Samudragupta → Prayaga Prashasti

12. Prayaga Pillar

  • The inscription was engraved on an ancient pillar at Prayaga.
  • The same pillar also contains inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka.
  • It is today located at Prayagraj.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Ashokan Pillar + Samudragupta Inscription → Prayaga

13. Harishena

  • The Prayaga Prashasti was composed by Harishena.
  • Harishena was an important officer and court poet of Samudragupta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harishena → Prayaga Prashasti

14. Language of Prayaga Prashasti

  • The inscription is in Sanskrit.
  • It is written in Gupta Brahmi script.
  • It combines prose and verse.

15. Information from Prayaga Prashasti

It records:

  • Samudragupta's genealogy.
  • His military campaigns.
  • Conquered rulers.
  • Frontier states.
  • Tribal republics.
  • Foreign rulers.
  • Personal accomplishments.

16. Samudragupta's Military Policy

Samudragupta did not treat every conquered region in the same way.

His policy differed according to:

  • Political importance.
  • Distance from the Gupta core.
  • Strategic conditions.

17. Aryavarta Policy

  • Several rulers of northern India were defeated.
  • Their kingdoms were more directly incorporated into Gupta-controlled territory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aryavarta Kings → Defeated and Kingdoms Annexed/Uprooted

18. Nine Aryavarta Kings

The Prayaga Prashasti names rulers including:

  • Rudradeva.
  • Matila.
  • Nagadatta.
  • Chandravarman.
  • Ganapatinaga.
  • Nagasena.
  • Achyuta.
  • Nandin.
  • Balavarman.

19. Dakshinapatha Campaign

  • Samudragupta conducted an important military expedition into southern India.
  • Twelve rulers of Dakshinapatha are listed in the Prayaga inscription.

20. Policy Toward Southern Kings

Samudragupta generally:

  • Defeated them.
  • Captured them.
  • Released them.
  • Restored their kingdoms.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dakshinapatha → Defeat + Release + Restoration

21. Why Southern Kingdoms Were Restored

  • Direct administration of distant southern territories would have been difficult.
  • Restoring defeated rulers allowed Samudragupta to claim political superiority without permanent occupation.

22. Twelve Dakshinapatha Rulers

The inscription names:

  • Mahendra of Kosala.
  • Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara.
  • Mantaraja of Kaurala.
  • Mahendragiri of Pishtapura.
  • Svamidatta of Kottura.
  • Damana of Erandapalla.
  • Vishnugopa of Kanchi.
  • Nilaraja of Avamukta.
  • Hastivarman of Vengi.
  • Ugrasena of Palakka.
  • Kubera of Devarashtra.
  • Dhananjaya of Kusthalapura.
📌 TNPSC High-Yield

Samudragupta's Southern Campaign → 12 Rulers

23. Vishnugopa of Kanchi

  • Vishnugopa was a Pallava ruler of Kanchi.
  • He was defeated by Samudragupta during the southern campaign.
  • Samudragupta restored him rather than annexing Kanchi permanently.
🔗 Tamil Nadu / South India Key Link

Samudragupta → Defeated Pallava Vishnugopa of Kanchi

24. Hastivarman of Vengi

  • Hastivarman of Vengi was another southern ruler defeated by Samudragupta.
  • Vengi was located in the eastern Deccan.

25. Atavika States

  • Samudragupta subdued rulers of forest regions described as Atavika states.
  • These areas lay between the northern core and the eastern/southern regions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atavika → Forest Kingdoms

26. Frontier States

The Prayaga Prashasti refers to frontier states such as:

  • Samatata.
  • Davaka.
  • Kamarupa.
  • Nepal.
  • Karttripura.

27. Samatata

  • Samatata was located in southeastern Bengal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Samatata → Bengal

28. Davaka

  • Davaka was located in the Assam region.

29. Kamarupa

  • Kamarupa was an important ancient kingdom of Assam.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kamarupa → Assam

30. Nepal

  • Nepal was among the frontier polities that acknowledged Gupta supremacy.

31. Tribal Republics

The inscription mentions political groups such as:

  • Malavas.
  • Arjunayanas.
  • Yaudheyas.
  • Madrakas.
  • Abhiras.
  • Sanakanikas.
  • Kakas.
  • Kharaparikas.

32. Yaudheyas

  • Yaudheyas were a powerful republican/tribal political group of northwestern India.
  • They had earlier issued their own coins.

33. Foreign Relations

The Prayaga inscription refers to foreign rulers such as:

  • Daivaputra-Shahi-Shahanushahi.
  • Saka-Murundas.
  • Rulers of Simhala.
  • Other island rulers.

These rulers sought diplomatic relations or acknowledged Samudragupta's prestige.

34. Simhala

  • Simhala refers to Sri Lanka.
  • The inscription indicates diplomatic relations between Samudragupta and the ruler of Sri Lanka.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simhala → Sri Lanka

35. Samudragupta and Sri Lanka

  • Sri Lankan ruler Meghavarna is traditionally associated with a request for permission to establish a monastery near Bodh Gaya.
  • This reflects diplomatic and Buddhist connections across the Indian Ocean.

36. "Napoleon of India"

  • Historian V. A. Smith called Samudragupta the "Napoleon of India" because of his extensive military campaigns.
📌 Must-Memorise

"Napoleon of India" → Samudragupta → V. A. Smith

37. Samudragupta's Ashvamedha

  • Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
  • Special coins commemorated the ceremony.
📌 Must-Memorise

Samudragupta → Ashvamedha Coins

38. Ashvamedha

  • Ashvamedha was an ancient royal horse sacrifice associated with political sovereignty and prestige.

39. Samudragupta as Musician

  • Some gold coins depict Samudragupta playing a stringed instrument, usually interpreted as a veena or lyre-like instrument.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lyrist/Veena Coins → Samudragupta

40. Samudragupta's Coin Types

Important types include:

  • Archer.
  • Battle-axe.
  • Tiger-slayer.
  • Lyrist.
  • Ashvamedha.

41. Kaviraja

  • Samudragupta is described as Kaviraja, meaning king among poets or poet-king.
  • This suggests literary accomplishment in addition to military achievements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kaviraja → Samudragupta

42. Religious Policy of Samudragupta

  • Samudragupta followed Brahmanical traditions.
  • He performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
  • Evidence also shows tolerance toward Buddhism and other traditions.

43. Ramagupta

  • Some literary and epigraphic evidence refers to a ruler named Ramagupta.
  • He may have ruled between Samudragupta and Chandragupta II.
  • His precise position in Gupta chronology remains debated.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Ramagupta → Possible Gupta Ruler, Historical Position Debated

44. Chandragupta II

  • Chandragupta II became one of the most powerful Gupta emperors.
  • He is commonly identified with the title Vikramaditya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandragupta II → Vikramaditya

45. Chandragupta II's Expansion

His major achievement was the conquest of:

  • Western Kshatrapas.
  • Gujarat.
  • Malwa.
  • Parts of western India.

46. Western Kshatrapas

  • Western Kshatrapas were Saka rulers of western India.
  • Their defeat gave the Guptas access to important western trade routes and ports.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandragupta II → Defeated Western Kshatrapas

47. Western Expansion

After conquering the Western Kshatrapas, Gupta influence reached:

  • Gujarat.
  • Malwa.
  • Arabian Sea coast.

48. Ujjain

  • Ujjain became a major Gupta political, commercial and cultural centre in western India.
  • It was strategically located on major trade routes.

49. Chandragupta II's Marriage Alliances

  • Chandragupta II used marriage alliances to strengthen political relations.
  • His daughter Prabhavatigupta married Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II.
📌 Must-Memorise

Prabhavatigupta → Vakataka Marriage Alliance

50. Prabhavatigupta

  • Prabhavatigupta was the daughter of Chandragupta II.
  • After Rudrasena II's death, she acted as regent in the Vakataka kingdom for her young sons.
  • Her inscriptions emphasise her Gupta lineage.

51. Gupta–Vakataka Alliance

  • The Vakatakas controlled important parts of the Deccan.
  • The marriage strengthened Gupta influence toward central and southern India.

52. Fa-Hien

  • Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during Chandragupta II's reign.
  • His journey is generally dated approximately 399–414 CE.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fa-Hien → Chandragupta II

53. Purpose of Fa-Hien's Visit

  • Fa-Hien travelled mainly to collect Buddhist scriptures and visit sacred Buddhist sites.
  • He was not primarily a political historian.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Fa-Hien → Buddhist Pilgrim, Not Royal Court Historian

54. Fa-Hien's Travel in India

He visited regions including:

  • Mathura.
  • Pataliputra.
  • Buddhist sacred sites.
  • Tamralipti.

55. Pataliputra

  • Fa-Hien spent considerable time at Pataliputra.
  • He studied Buddhist texts and described monasteries and social conditions.

56. Tamralipti

  • Tamralipti was an important ancient port in Bengal.
  • Fa-Hien travelled from there by sea toward Sri Lanka.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamralipti → Ancient Bengal Port

57. Fa-Hien on Society

Fa-Hien's account refers to:

  • Prosperous settlements.
  • Buddhist institutions.
  • Charitable establishments.
  • Social exclusion of Chandalas in certain regions.

His descriptions should be read in the context of his religious interests.

58. Mehrauli Iron Pillar

  • The famous Iron Pillar is located at Mehrauli in Delhi.
  • Its inscription praises a king named Chandra.
  • This king is commonly identified with Chandragupta II, although the identification is not absolutely certain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iron Pillar → Mehrauli → King Chandra

59. Importance of Iron Pillar

  • The pillar demonstrates advanced ancient Indian ironworking.
  • It is famous for remarkable resistance to corrosion.

60. Udayagiri Caves

  • Udayagiri caves are located near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh.
  • They contain important Gupta-period Hindu sculptures and inscriptions.
  • Chandragupta II is associated with the site.

61. Udayagiri Varaha

  • A famous monumental relief depicts Vishnu's Varaha incarnation rescuing the Earth.
  • It is one of the best-known examples of Gupta-period religious art.
📌 Must-Memorise

Udayagiri → Varaha Relief

62. Chandragupta II Coinage

Important types include:

  • Archer.
  • Lion-slayer.
  • Horseman and other varieties.
  • Silver coins based partly on western Kshatrapa models after his conquest of western India.

63. Gupta Silver Coins

  • Silver coinage became especially important after Chandragupta II conquered the Western Kshatrapas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gupta Silver Coins → Western Kshatrapa Conquest

64. Kumaragupta I

  • Kumaragupta I succeeded Chandragupta II.
  • He ruled for a long period during the fifth century CE.
  • He used the title Mahendraditya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kumaragupta I → Mahendraditya

65. Kumaragupta I and Empire

  • The Gupta Empire remained extensive during his reign.
  • Several inscriptions and coins indicate continuing administrative stability.

66. Kumaragupta Coinage

His coins include representations associated with:

  • Archer.
  • Horseman.
  • Elephant.
  • Peacock/Karttikeya themes.

67. Nalanda and Kumaragupta I

  • Nalanda developed into a major Buddhist monastic and educational centre during the Gupta period.
  • Later tradition associates its foundation or major early patronage with Kumaragupta I.
  • The precise founding history is not completely certain.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Nalanda → Major Gupta-Period Centre; Kumaragupta Association Traditional

68. Nalanda

  • Nalanda was located in present-day Bihar.
  • It later became one of the most famous Buddhist centres of learning in Asia.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nalanda → Bihar

69. Skandagupta

  • Skandagupta succeeded Kumaragupta I.
  • He was the last major Gupta ruler able to maintain extensive imperial authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

Last Great Gupta Ruler → Skandagupta

70. Skandagupta and the Hunas

  • Skandagupta successfully resisted early Huna attacks.
  • Huna pressure nevertheless became a major long-term threat to Gupta power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Skandagupta → Repelled Hunas

71. Bhitari Pillar Inscription

  • The Bhitari Pillar inscription is an important source for Skandagupta.
  • It records his military accomplishments and dynastic position.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhitari Inscription → Skandagupta

72. Junagadh Inscription

  • Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription is another major source.
  • It is located in Gujarat.
📌 Must-Memorise

Junagadh Inscription → Skandagupta

73. Sudarshana Lake

  • Sudarshana Lake in Gujarat had an ancient history extending back to the Mauryan period.
  • During Skandagupta's reign, its embankment was repaired after damage.

74. Parnadatta

  • Skandagupta appointed Parnadatta as governor of Saurashtra.

75. Chakrapalita

  • Chakrapalita, son of Parnadatta, supervised repairs to Sudarshana Lake.
  • The event is recorded in the Junagadh inscription.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sudarshana Lake Repair → Chakrapalita → Skandagupta Period

76. Later Imperial Guptas

After Skandagupta, rulers included figures such as:

  • Purugupta.
  • Kumaragupta II.
  • Budhagupta.
  • Narasimhagupta.
  • Kumaragupta III.
  • Vishnugupta.

The succession sequence is complex and not equally clear for every ruler.

77. Budhagupta

  • Budhagupta ruled during the later fifth century CE.
  • His inscriptions show that Gupta authority still extended over important regions, though imperial power was weakening.

78. Narasimhagupta Baladitya

  • Narasimhagupta is also known as Baladitya.
  • Later Buddhist traditions associate him with conflict involving Huna ruler Mihirakula.
  • Details come from later sources and must be used cautiously.

79. Imperial Guptas vs Later Guptas

  • The "Later Guptas" of Magadha were a separate ruling family that emerged after the decline of the imperial Gupta dynasty.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Later Guptas ≠ Same as Imperial Gupta Dynasty

80. Gupta Administration

The Gupta state was a monarchy.

Important characteristics included:

  • Hereditary kingship.
  • Ministers and high officials.
  • Provincial administration.
  • District administration.
  • Village administration.
  • Increasing role of local elites.

81. King

The emperor was:

  • Supreme military authority.
  • Highest administrative authority.
  • Important judicial authority.

Gupta kings used grand titles.

82. Gupta Royal Titles

Titles included:

  • Maharajadhiraja.
  • Paramabhattaraka.
  • Parameshvara.

83. Council and Ministers

  • Kings were assisted by ministers and high-ranking officials.
  • Some offices could be held by members of influential families across generations.

84. Kumaramatya

  • Kumaramatyas were high-ranking Gupta officials.
  • They performed important administrative duties.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kumaramatya → High Gupta Official

85. Sandhivigrahika

  • Sandhivigrahika was an official associated with matters of peace, war and diplomatic agreements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sandhivigrahika → Peace and War / Foreign Affairs

86. Mahadandanayaka

  • Mahadandanayaka was a high-ranking official associated with military and/or judicial authority depending on context.

87. Harishena's Offices

Harishena held titles including:

  • Kumaramatya.
  • Sandhivigrahika.
  • Mahadandanayaka.

This demonstrates that important officers could combine several responsibilities.

88. Provinces

  • Gupta provinces were commonly called Bhuktis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Province → Bhukti

89. Uparika

  • The governor of a Bhukti was commonly known as an Uparika.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhukti → Uparika

90. District

  • Districts were commonly called Vishayas.
📌 Must-Memorise

District → Vishaya

91. Vishayapati

  • A Vishayapati administered a Vishaya or district.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vishaya → Vishayapati

92. Village

  • The village was generally called Grama.
  • It remained the basic rural unit.

93. Village Head

  • Village administration involved local headmen and elders.
  • The exact titles varied by region and inscription.

94. Damodarpur Copper Plates

  • Damodarpur copper-plate inscriptions from Bengal are important sources for Gupta administration.
  • They provide information on:
  • Bhuktis.
  • Vishayas.
  • Officials.
  • Land transactions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Damodarpur Plates → Gupta Administration

95. Local District Committee

Records show participation by local representatives such as:

  • Nagara-shreshthin.
  • Sarthavaha.
  • Prathama-kulika.
  • Prathama-kayastha.

96. Nagara-Shreshthin

  • Nagara-shreshthin was an important chief merchant or banker of the town.

97. Sarthavaha

  • Sarthavaha was associated with merchant caravans and long-distance trade.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarthavaha → Caravan Merchant Leader

98. Prathama-Kulika

  • Prathama-kulika represented leading artisans or craftsmen.

99. Prathama-Kayastha

  • Prathama-kayastha was associated with administrative record keeping or scribal functions.

100. Decentralisation

  • Local authorities and regional elites had significant administrative roles.
  • Land grants increasingly transferred certain fiscal or administrative privileges to beneficiaries.
  • Historians debate the extent to which this represented "feudalisation."
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Gupta Administration → Less Centralised Than Mauryan Model

101. Land Grants

Land grants were made to:

  • Brahmanas.
  • Religious institutions.
  • Officials in some contexts.

Many grants were recorded on copper plates.

102. Agrahara

  • Agrahara commonly referred to land or a village granted to Brahmanas, often with revenue privileges.

103. Effects of Land Grants

Land grants could transfer:

  • Revenue rights.
  • Administrative privileges.
  • Control over certain local resources.

Their importance increased in the post-Gupta period.

104. Gupta Revenue

Important revenue terms included:

  • Bhaga.
  • Bhoga.
  • Kara.
  • Hiranya.

Exact meaning could vary across documents and regions.

105. Bhaga

  • Bhaga generally referred to the ruler's share of agricultural produce.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhaga → Share of Produce

106. Bhoga

  • Bhoga generally referred to supplies, provisions or customary dues provided to rulers or officials.

107. Kara

  • Kara broadly referred to taxes or tribute.

108. Hiranya

  • Hiranya usually referred to payments made in cash or money rather than kind.

109. Gupta Army

Major components included:

  • Infantry.
  • Cavalry.
  • Elephants.

Cavalry played an increasingly important military role in this period.

110. Gupta Coinage

  • Gupta rulers issued abundant gold coins.
  • These coins are commonly called dinars in modern historical literature.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gupta Gold Coins → Dinars

111. Importance of Gupta Coins

Coins provide information on:

  • Royal titles.
  • Religion.
  • Military achievements.
  • Art.
  • Political propaganda.
  • Economy.

112. Gold Coins

  • Early and high-imperial Gupta gold coinage was famous for high artistic quality.
  • Later issues show changes in weight and metal quality.

113. Garuda Emblem

  • Garuda was an important Gupta dynastic and Vaishnava symbol.
  • It appears on coins, seals and standards.
📌 Must-Memorise

Guptas → Garuda Emblem

114. King–Queen Coin

  • Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi appear on the famous King–Queen type.

115. Lyrist Coin

  • Samudragupta is shown playing a musical instrument.

116. Ashvamedha Coin

  • Samudragupta's Ashvamedha coins commemorate his horse sacrifice.

117. Archer Type

  • Archer-type gold coins were issued by several Gupta rulers.
  • They depict the king holding a bow.

118. Economy

The Gupta economy rested on:

  • Agriculture.
  • Crafts.
  • Trade.
  • Guilds.
  • Tax revenue.
  • Urban and rural production.

119. Agriculture

  • Agriculture was the economic foundation of the empire.
  • Major crops included:
  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Pulses.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Oilseeds.

120. Irrigation

Agricultural water came from:

  • Wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Rivers.
  • Local irrigation works.

Sudarshana Lake is an important inscriptional example of water management.

121. Craft Production

Important crafts included:

  • Textiles.
  • Metalworking.
  • Jewellery.
  • Pottery.
  • Ivory work.
  • Stone carving.

122. Guilds

  • Merchant and artisan guilds remained important economic institutions.
  • Guilds could:
  • Organise production.
  • Manage collective funds.
  • Make religious donations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Guild → Shreni

123. Mandsaur Silk Weavers

  • An inscription from Mandsaur records a guild of silk weavers.
  • The guild migrated and became an important economic group.
  • It contributed to the construction and repair of a Sun temple.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mandsaur Inscription → Silk Weavers' Guild

124. Trade

Trade occurred through:

  • Land routes.
  • River routes.
  • Coastal routes.
  • Overseas networks.

125. Western Trade Advantage

  • Chandragupta II's conquest of Gujarat and western India improved Gupta access to Arabian Sea trade routes.

126. Roman Trade

  • India's direct trade with the Roman Mediterranean changed considerably after the earlier Kushana-Satavahana period.
  • Long-distance trade did not disappear completely.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gupta Age → Do Not Say "Foreign Trade Completely Stopped"

127. Society

Gupta society contained:

  • Brahmanas.
  • Rulers and warriors.
  • Merchants.
  • Artisans.
  • Peasants.
  • Labouring communities.
  • Numerous jatis and occupational groups.

128. Varna and Jati

  • Brahmanical texts emphasised the four-varna framework.
  • Actual society consisted of many jatis, occupations and regional communities.

129. Chandalas

  • Fa-Hien describes Chandalas as socially segregated in parts of northern India.
  • His account is an important source for social exclusion during the period.

130. Position of Women

Evidence suggests:

  • Patriarchal family structures remained strong.
  • Early marriage became increasingly encouraged in Brahmanical normative texts.
  • Women possessed certain property rights such as stridhana.
  • Conditions varied according to social group and region.

131. Stridhana

  • Stridhana referred to certain forms of property legally recognised as belonging to a woman.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stridhana → Woman's Property

132. Sati Evidence

  • The Eran inscription dated 510 CE is commonly cited as the earliest known epigraphic evidence for sati.
  • It records the wife of Goparaja following him in death.
📌 Must-Memorise

Early Epigraphic Sati Evidence → Eran → 510 CE

133. Eran

  • Eran is located in present-day Madhya Pradesh.
  • It has produced several important Gupta-period inscriptions and monuments.

134. Education

Important centres included:

  • Pataliputra.
  • Ujjain.
  • Nalanda.
  • Monasteries and Brahmanical learning centres.

135. Sanskrit

  • Sanskrit became a major language of:
  • Court inscriptions.
  • Literature.
  • Scholarship.
  • Gupta royal inscriptions are especially associated with polished Sanskrit.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gupta Court Culture → Sanskrit

136. Literature

The Gupta/classical age saw major development in:

  • Poetry.
  • Drama.
  • Grammar.
  • Lexicography.
  • Religious literature.

137. Kalidasa

  • Kalidasa is traditionally associated with the Gupta age.
  • He is regarded as one of the greatest Sanskrit poets and dramatists.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kalidasa → Gupta-Age Sanskrit Literature

138. Important Works of Kalidasa

Major works include:

  • Abhijnanashakuntalam.
  • Meghaduta.
  • Raghuvamsha.
  • Kumarasambhava.
  • Malavikagnimitram.
  • Vikramorvashiyam.

139. Abhijnanashakuntalam

  • Abhijnanashakuntalam is a Sanskrit drama based on the story of Shakuntala and Dushyanta.

140. Meghaduta

  • Meghaduta is a lyrical poem in which a cloud carries the message of an exiled Yaksha.

141. Raghuvamsha

  • Raghuvamsha is an epic poem about the Raghu dynasty.

142. Kumarasambhava

  • Kumarasambhava narrates themes surrounding the birth of Kumara/Kartikeya.

143. Vishakhadatta

  • Vishakhadatta is traditionally associated with classical Sanskrit drama.
  • His exact date is uncertain.

144. Mudrarakshasa

  • Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta deals with the rise of Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mudrarakshasa → Mauryan Story, But Author Belongs to a Much Later Classical Period

145. Amarasimha

  • Amarasimha is traditionally associated with the Sanskrit lexicon Amarakosha.
  • His exact court association is less certain than later legends suggest.

146. Amarakosha

  • Amarakosha is an important Sanskrit thesaurus or lexicon.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amarasimha → Amarakosha

147. Navaratnas Tradition

  • Later tradition speaks of nine gems, or Navaratnas, at Vikramaditya's court.
  • The historicity of the complete traditional list is not securely established.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Navaratnas of Vikramaditya → Later Tradition, Not Fully Historical

148. Puranas

  • Many Puranic texts were compiled, edited or expanded over long periods including the Gupta age.
  • They contributed to the development of Brahmanical religious traditions.

149. Smritis

  • Dharmashastra and Smriti traditions continued to develop during the period.
  • They discussed:
  • Social duties.
  • Law.
  • Inheritance.
  • Social norms.

150. Science and Mathematics

The Gupta age is famous for developments in:

  • Mathematics.
  • Astronomy.
  • Metallurgy.
  • Medicine.

151. Aryabhata

  • Aryabhata was one of ancient India's greatest mathematicians and astronomers.
  • He was born in 476 CE.
  • His major work Aryabhatiya was composed in 499 CE.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aryabhata → Aryabhatiya → 499 CE

152. Aryabhatiya

The Aryabhatiya deals with:

  • Arithmetic.
  • Algebraic methods.
  • Geometry.
  • Trigonometry.
  • Astronomy.

153. Earth's Rotation

  • Aryabhata correctly explained that the apparent daily movement of the stars is related to Earth's rotation on its axis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aryabhata → Earth Rotates on Axis

154. Eclipse Explanation

  • Aryabhata explained solar and lunar eclipses scientifically in terms of shadows rather than mythological causes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aryabhata → Scientific Explanation of Eclipses

155. Value of Pi

  • Aryabhata gave a remarkably accurate approximation of π, close to 3.1416.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aryabhata → π ≈ 3.1416

156. Aryabhata and Zero — Trap

  • Aryabhata made major mathematical contributions.
  • It is inaccurate to simply state that he "invented zero."
  • The Indian place-value and zero tradition developed over time.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Aryabhata ≠ Proven Inventor of Zero

157. Decimal Place-Value System

  • Indian mathematics made major progress toward the decimal place-value system during the classical period.
  • This later had enormous influence on world mathematics.

158. Varahamihira

  • Varahamihira flourished in the sixth century CE at Ujjain.
  • He belongs broadly to the late Gupta/post-Gupta classical intellectual world.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Varahamihira → 6th Century, Broad Classical Age

159. Works of Varahamihira

Important works include:

  • Brihat Samhita.
  • Pancha-Siddhantika.

160. Metallurgy

Gupta-era metallurgical skill is demonstrated by:

  • High-quality gold coinage.
  • Iron working.
  • Mehrauli Iron Pillar.

161. Religion

Major religious traditions included:

  • Vaishnavism.
  • Shaivism.
  • Buddhism.
  • Jainism.

162. Gupta Royal Religion

  • Several Gupta rulers were devotees of Vishnu.
  • Titles such as Parama-Bhagavata occur.
  • Garuda became a prominent dynastic emblem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gupta Royal Symbol → Garuda → Vaishnava Association

163. Religious Tolerance

  • Brahmanical traditions received strong royal patronage.
  • Buddhism and Jainism also continued.
  • Different religious communities coexisted across the empire.

164. Vaishnavism

Evidence includes:

  • Garuda symbols.
  • Vishnu temples.
  • Varaha sculptures.
  • Royal titles.

165. Shaivism

  • Shaiva worship also flourished.
  • Shiva images and shrines are known from the Gupta period.

166. Buddhism

  • Buddhist monasteries remained active.
  • Fa-Hien visited numerous Buddhist sites.
  • Nalanda developed into a major monastic centre.

167. Jainism

  • Jain communities continued particularly in commercial and urban centres.
  • Jain images and inscriptions survive from the broader Gupta period.

168. Temple Architecture

The Gupta period was important in the development of structural Hindu temples.

Features included:

  • Square sanctum.
  • Entrance porch.
  • Increasingly prominent superstructure.
  • Sculptured doorways.

169. Garbhagriha

  • Garbhagriha is the inner sanctum containing the principal deity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Garbhagriha → Sanctum

170. Early Nagara Development

  • Gupta temples contributed to the evolution of the northern Indian Nagara temple tradition.
  • Later Nagara temples developed increasingly elaborate shikharas.

171. Dashavatara Temple

  • The Dashavatara Temple is located at Deogarh in present-day Uttar Pradesh.
  • It is dedicated to Vishnu.
  • It is an important early structural temple.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dashavatara Temple → Deogarh → Vishnu

172. Deogarh Temple

Important features include:

  • Square sanctum.
  • Sculptured panels.
  • Early shikhara form.
  • Vaishnava themes.

173. Anantasayana Vishnu

  • A famous relief at Deogarh depicts Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta.

174. Bhitargaon Temple

  • Bhitargaon Temple is located in Uttar Pradesh.
  • It is one of the important surviving ancient brick temples.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhitargaon → Brick Temple

175. Tigawa Temple

  • Tigawa in Madhya Pradesh contains an important Gupta-period Vishnu temple.

176. Sanchi Temple 17

  • Temple 17 at Sanchi is an important example of simple Gupta-period structural temple architecture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sanchi Temple 17 → Gupta Architecture

177. Sculpture

Gupta sculpture is characterised by:

  • Balanced proportions.
  • Spiritual expression.
  • Refined modelling.
  • Simple elegance.

178. Sarnath School

  • Sarnath became an important centre of Gupta Buddhist sculpture.
  • Buddha images often display:
  • Smooth modelling.
  • Thin robes.
  • Calm expression.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarnath → Gupta Buddha Sculpture

179. Mathura School

  • Mathura continued as another important sculpture centre.
  • It developed from earlier Kushana artistic traditions.

180. Gupta Buddha Images

Typical features include:

  • Serene expression.
  • Refined body modelling.
  • Halo.
  • Symbolic hand gestures.

181. Mudra

  • Mudra means a symbolic hand gesture in Indian religious art.

Examples include:

  • Abhaya mudra.
  • Dharmachakra mudra.

182. Ajanta — Important Caution

  • Many famous Ajanta paintings belong to the fifth-century Vakataka period.
  • They are contemporary with the Guptas but were not simply products of direct Gupta imperial patronage.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ajanta Paintings → Gupta-Age Style/Contemporary, Largely Vakataka Patronage

183. Gupta Art Characteristics

Gupta-period art combined:

  • Religious symbolism.
  • Technical refinement.
  • Idealised human form.
  • Controlled ornamentation.

184. Inscriptions — Major Gupta Sources

Important inscriptions include:

  • Prayaga Prashasti.
  • Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription.
  • Udayagiri inscriptions.
  • Bhitari Pillar inscription.
  • Junagadh inscription.
  • Damodarpur copper plates.
  • Eran inscriptions.
  • Bilsad inscription.

185. Bilsad Inscription

  • Bilsad Pillar inscription is associated with Kumaragupta I.
  • It provides information about Gupta genealogy and rule.

186. Gupta Script

  • Gupta inscriptions were generally written in a developed form of Brahmi script.
  • Later northern Indian scripts evolved partly from this tradition.

187. Gupta Language

  • Sanskrit increasingly became the prestigious language of royal inscriptions.
  • Prakrit continued in broader social and religious use in various regions.

188. Gupta Calendar

  • Gupta-era dates are found in inscriptions.
  • Conversion into Common Era dates usually begins from 319–320 CE.

189. Causes of Gupta Decline

Important factors included:

  • Huna invasions.
  • Succession disputes.
  • Weak later rulers.
  • Regional rebellions.
  • Growth of independent powers.
  • Fiscal and administrative decentralisation.

190. Huna Invasions

  • Central Asian Huna groups entered northwestern India.
  • Skandagupta initially resisted them successfully.
  • Later invasions weakened Gupta political authority.

191. Toramana

  • Toramana was an important Huna ruler.
  • He established authority over parts of northwestern and central India as Gupta control weakened.
📌 Must-Memorise

Toramana → Huna Ruler

192. Mihirakula

  • Mihirakula succeeded Toramana.
  • He became one of the best-known Huna rulers in Indian historical sources.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mihirakula → Huna Ruler

193. Yasodharman

  • Yasodharman of Malwa emerged as a powerful regional ruler in the sixth century.
  • His rise further demonstrated the fragmentation of Gupta imperial authority.
  • He is associated with victory over Mihirakula.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Yasodharman → Malwa → Defeated Mihirakula

194. Decentralisation and Decline

Increasing political power of:

  • Governors.
  • Local chiefs.
  • Landholders.
  • Regional dynasties.

reduced central imperial control.

195. Loss of Western India

  • Western territories were economically and strategically valuable.
  • Loss of control over these regions weakened Gupta revenues and trade connections.

196. Regional Powers After the Guptas

Important post-Gupta powers included:

  • Maukharis.
  • Later Guptas.
  • Pushyabhutis.
  • Maitrakas.
  • Aulikara rulers.

197. Maitrakas

  • Maitrakas established an important kingdom centred at Valabhi in Gujarat after Gupta power weakened.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maitrakas → Valabhi

198. Valabhi

  • Valabhi became an important political and educational centre of western India.

199. Gupta Political Legacy

The Guptas influenced later Indian states through:

  • Royal titles.
  • Administrative terminology.
  • Sanskrit court culture.
  • Coin traditions.
  • Religious patronage.

200. Gupta Cultural Legacy

Major legacies include:

  • Classical Sanskrit literature.
  • Temple architecture.
  • Sculpture.
  • Mathematics.
  • Astronomy.
  • Metallurgy.

201. Gupta–South India Link

The most important direct political link for TNPSC is:

  • Samudragupta's southern expedition.
  • Defeat of Pallava ruler Vishnugopa of Kanchi.
  • Restoration of the southern kingdom rather than permanent annexation.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Gupta–Tamil/South Link → Samudragupta vs Vishnugopa of Kanchi

202. Gupta vs Pallavas

  • The Guptas did not establish lasting direct rule over Kanchi.
  • Pallava political development continued in South India.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Samudragupta Defeated Kanchi ≠ Guptas Permanently Annexed Tamil Region

203. Major Ruler–Achievement Pairings

  • Sri Gupta → Earliest known founder.
  • Chandragupta I → Lichchhavi alliance.
  • Samudragupta → Extensive conquests.
  • Chandragupta II → Defeated Western Kshatrapas.
  • Kumaragupta I → Long stable reign.
  • Skandagupta → Resisted Hunas.

204. Major Ruler–Title Pairings

  • Chandragupta I → Maharajadhiraja.
  • Samudragupta → Kaviraja.
  • Chandragupta II → Vikramaditya.
  • Kumaragupta I → Mahendraditya.

205. Ruler–Source Pairings

  • Samudragupta → Prayaga Prashasti.
  • Chandragupta II → Fa-Hien / Udayagiri / King Chandra inscription association.
  • Kumaragupta I → Bilsad inscription.
  • Skandagupta → Bhitari + Junagadh inscriptions.

206. Source–Author Pairings

  • Prayaga Prashasti → Harishena.
  • Aryabhatiya → Aryabhata.
  • Amarakosha → Amarasimha.
  • Abhijnanashakuntalam → Kalidasa.
  • Mudrarakshasa → Vishakhadatta.

207. Place–Feature Pairings

  • Prayaga → Samudragupta inscription.
  • Udayagiri → Varaha relief.
  • Mehrauli → Iron Pillar.
  • Deogarh → Dashavatara Temple.
  • Bhitargaon → Brick temple.
  • Sarnath → Buddha sculpture.
  • Nalanda → Buddhist learning.
  • Mandsaur → Silk weavers.
  • Eran → Early sati inscription.
  • Junagadh → Sudarshana Lake repairs.

208. Administration Pairings

  • Province → Bhukti.
  • Governor → Uparika.
  • District → Vishaya.
  • District head → Vishayapati.
  • Village → Grama.
  • High official → Kumaramatya.
  • Peace/war official → Sandhivigrahika.
  • Merchant leader → Sarthavaha.

209. Revenue Pairings

  • Bhaga → Share of produce.
  • Bhoga → Supplies/customary dues.
  • Kara → Tax/tribute.
  • Hiranya → Cash payment.

210. Culture Pairings

  • Kalidasa → Sanskrit literature.
  • Aryabhata → Mathematics and astronomy.
  • Iron Pillar → Metallurgy.
  • Sarnath → Sculpture.
  • Deogarh → Temple architecture.
  • Garuda → Gupta dynastic symbol.

211. Coin Pairings

  • King–Queen → Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi.
  • Lyrist → Samudragupta.
  • Ashvamedha → Samudragupta.
  • Silver Kshatrapa-style coins → Chandragupta II after western conquest.
  • Gold dinars → Gupta imperial coinage.

212. TNPSC Common Doubts

Who founded Gupta political greatness? → Chandragupta I.

Who was earliest known Gupta ruler? → Sri Gupta.

Who was greatest conqueror? → Samudragupta.

Who defeated Western Kshatrapas? → Chandragupta II.

Who resisted Hunas? → Skandagupta.

Who visited during Chandragupta II? → Fa-Hien.

213. TNPSC Traps

  • Sri Gupta and Chandragupta I are not the same person.
  • Sri Gupta is the earliest known ruler; Chandragupta I created major imperial power.
  • Gupta Era begins in 319–320 CE.
  • Chandragupta I married Kumaradevi, a Lichchhavi princess.
  • Prayaga Prashasti belongs to Samudragupta.
  • Harishena composed the Prayaga Prashasti.
  • Samudragupta annexed northern kingdoms more directly but restored many southern rulers.
  • Vishnugopa of Kanchi was defeated but restored.
  • "Napoleon of India" refers to Samudragupta.
  • Chandragupta II is associated with Vikramaditya.
  • Chandragupta II defeated Western Kshatrapas.
  • Fa-Hien visited during Chandragupta II.
  • Fa-Hien was a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim.
  • Kumaragupta I used the title Mahendraditya.
  • Skandagupta resisted Huna invasions.
  • Bhitari and Junagadh inscriptions are linked with Skandagupta.
  • Sudarshana Lake repairs were supervised by Chakrapalita.
  • Bhukti means province.
  • Vishaya means district.
  • Uparika means provincial governor.
  • Gupta gold coins are commonly called dinars.
  • Garuda was a major Gupta symbol.
  • Aryabhata did not simply "invent zero."
  • Aryabhatiya was written in 499 CE.
  • Kalidasa is associated with Gupta-age Sanskrit culture.
  • Ajanta's famous fifth-century phase was mainly under Vakataka patronage, not direct Gupta imperial patronage.
  • Eran 510 CE inscription is commonly cited for early epigraphic evidence of sati.
  • "Later Guptas" were a separate dynasty from the imperial Guptas.

214. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Sri Gupta → Founder.
  • Ghatotkacha → Maharaja.
  • Chandragupta I → Kumaradevi.
  • Gupta Era → 319–320.
  • Samudragupta → Harishena.
  • Prayaga → Conquests.
  • Kanchi → Vishnugopa.
  • Napoleon → Samudragupta.
  • Lyrist → Samudragupta.
  • Ashvamedha → Samudragupta.
  • Chandragupta II → Vikramaditya.
  • Kshatrapas → Defeated.
  • Fa-Hien → Chandragupta II.
  • Kumaragupta → Mahendraditya.
  • Skandagupta → Hunas.
  • Bhitari → Skandagupta.
  • Junagadh → Sudarshana.
  • Bhukti → Province.
  • Vishaya → District.
  • Garuda → Gupta.
  • Dinar → Gold.
  • Kalidasa → Literature.
  • Aryabhata → 499.
  • Deogarh → Vishnu temple.
  • Udayagiri → Varaha.
  • Mehrauli → Iron Pillar.
  • Eran → Sati 510.
  • Huna → Toramana/Mihirakula.

  • Who was Nagara-shreshthin? → Chief merchant/banker.
  • Who was Sarthavaha? → Caravan merchant leader.

  • Which ruler expanded silver coinage after defeating Western Kshatrapas? → Chandragupta II.
  • What was a guild called? → Shreni.
  • Which inscription records a silk-weavers' guild? → Mandsaur inscription.
  • Which language flourished as the principal court language? → Sanskrit.
  • Most famous Gupta-age Sanskrit poet? → Kalidasa.
  • Author of Abhijnanashakuntalam? → Kalidasa.
  • Author of Meghaduta? → Kalidasa.
  • Author of Raghuvamsha? → Kalidasa.
  • Author of Mudrarakshasa? → Vishakhadatta.
  • Mudrarakshasa concerns which historical ruler? → Chandragupta Maurya.

  • Who wrote Aryabhatiya? → Aryabhata.
